item.title: Continuously aligned biomimetic sites in MXene membranes for rapid lithium extraction
item.description: Efficient separation of lithium ions (Li +) from magnesium ions (Mg 2+) remains a central challenge for direct lithium extraction from salt lake brines due to their similar physicochemical properties. Inspired by biological ion channels, biomimetic membranes have been explored to improve Li + /Mg 2+ separation. However, most biomimetic membranes focus primarily on introducing recognition sites while overlooking the structural features of biological channels, particularly the continuous arrangement of coordination sites that facilitates efficient ion transport. Here, inspired by the continuous carbonyl coordination structure of the KcsA ion channel, 4-formylbenzo-15-crown-5 ether was periodically grafted onto poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) chains and integrated with MXene nanosheets to construct two-dimensional interlayer channels with continuously aligned crown ether recognition sites. This architecture shifts Li + transport from random diffusion to successive site-to-site hopping, reducing the effective transport energy barrier. The resulting biomimetic MXene membrane achieves a Li + flux of 0.12 mol·m −2 ·h −1 with Li + /Mg 2+ selectivity of 109 and performs effectively across various salt lake brines.

item.title: Sequential anion chemistry enables dynamic interphase regulation in high-voltage LiCoO 2
item.description: Lithium-ion batteries using LiCoO2 cathodes have powered portable electronics for decades, yet their operation above 4.5 volts remains severely constrained by the unstable evolution of the cathode-electrolyte interphase (CEI). Under high-voltage conditions, lattice oxygen release and continuous electrolyte oxidation progressively degrade interfacial integrity. Here, we report a diluent-mediated local solvation regulation strategy to decrease dissociative solvent molecules and induce dual anion selective redistribution around Li+, forming a sequential solvation motif that drives sequential anion interfacial chemistry. DFOB- preferentially decomposes to establish a robust initial CEI framework, while BF4- continuously drives interfacial reactions to dynamically repair CEI defects and quench reactive oxygen species generated from lattice oxygen release. This dynamic regulation mechanism effectively stabilizes LiCoO2 under aggressive high-voltage cycling. Consequently, the LiCoO2 cathode delivers stable performance for 500 cycles at 4.5 volts with 73.5% capacity retention even in a low-concentration ether-based electrolyte. Furthermore, graphite||LiCoO2 pouch cell achieves an energy density of 265.8 watt-hours per kilogram and exhibits favorable low-temperature resilience, retaining 99.1% capacity after 700 cycles at -20°C. These findings provide critical mechanistic insights into how solvation structure-driven anion chemistry can govern interfacial stability and unlock high-voltage, extreme-condition lithium-ion batteries.

item.title: Engineering interfacial nucleation and growth for long-life, ultrahigh-rate anode-free sodium batteries
item.description: The practical application of anode-free sodium batteries (AFSBs) is limited by the poor reversibility of sodium plating and stripping on current collectors. Here, we show that conventional graphite unexpectedly regulates sodium plating and stripping through a dynamic, interactive interface that enables multidimensional charge transport. This behavior arises from the combination of ultrafast mixed ion-electron transport, reversible ether solvent cointercalation, and the anisotropic flake architecture of graphite, which together promote efficient charge exchange and edge-dominant nucleation. The resulting adaptive interface forms an ultrathin, mechanically robust SEI that stabilizes sodium plating and stripping across a wide current density range (1C to 10C). Ampere hour-level anode-free pouch cells based on this design exhibit an initial Coulombic efficiency of 92.3%, retain 84.9% capacity after 1100 cycles at 3C, and display exceptional safety characteristics, including minimal temperature rise at high rates and no thermal runaway during nail penetration. These results establish a platform for controlling interfacial metal nucleation and growth in AFSBs.

item.title: Time-evolved hetero-alkali interphases enable long-life sulfide-based anode-free solid-state batteries
item.description: Sulfide-based anode-free solid-state batteries (AFSSBs) offer high energy density and improved safety, but their practical implementation is hindered by parasitic reactions between freshly plated lithium (Li) and sulfide solid electrolytes. These reactions continuously consume the limited cathode-derived Li inventory, increase interfacial impedance, and promote nonuniform Li plating and stripping. Here, sodium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (NaFSI) is incorporated into Li5.4PS4.4Cl1.6 (LPSC) to kinetically program interphase evolution. Heat treatment initially generates a NaF/LiF-rich interphase on the LPSC surface. This fluoride-rich region chemically stabilizes the interface and suppresses direct LPSC reduction. During the early cycles, the outermost region progressively evolves into a LiF/Li3N-rich layer, while the NaF-containing phase becomes buried beneath the Li-rich surface region, producing a time-evolved compositional gradient. Although NaF provides effective chemical passivation, its poor Li+ conductivity can impede interfacial ion transport. The subsequent formation of Li3N-rich domains, which exhibit substantially higher Li+ conductivity than NaF, provides more favorable transport pathways, homogenizes interfacial Li+ flux, and promotes uniform Li plating and stripping. This time-evolved gradient interphase therefore combines early-stage chemical stabilization and Li conservation with improved long-term ion transport kinetics, suppressing impedance growth, localized inactive Li accumulation, and filamentary shorting. Consequently, the AFSSB using the NaFSI-modified LPSC interlayer retains 77.6% of its capacity after 500 cycles at 0.2 C, whereas the cell with bare LPSC retains only 32.1% after 100 cycles. These findings establish temporally programmed gradient interphases as a general strategy for conserving active Li and stabilizing sulfide-based AFSSBs.

item.title: Battery-free ingestible electronic capsule with programmable high-output soft actuation for active gastrointestinal interventions
item.description: Ingestible capsules have garnered considerable attention due to their high gastrointestinal (GI) transitability and minimally invasive nature. However, constrained by pill-sized dimensions (approximately 2 to 4 cubic centimeters), current ingestible capsules face persistent challenges in achieving both controllable high mechanical output and sufficient onboard power delivery, limiting their capacity for effective in vivo therapeutic interventions. Here, we present a wirelessly powered ingestible electronic capsule that integrates programmable soft phase-change actuation within a rigid-soft architecture to enable programmable, high-output mechanical operations. Leveraging bidirectional thermoelectric regulation and guided rigid-soft coupling, the capsule delivers a peak force of 3.8 newtons and a volumetric stroke of ∼250 cubic millimeters within a confined geometry based on the phase-change actuation. To power this actuation, we implemented a compact wireless power transfer system that achieved a maximum load-received power per unit receiver-coil volume of 9.15 watts per cubic centimeter at a 5-centimeter transfer distance under the tested conditions. The structural adaptability of the soft actuator allows modular integration of functional end-effectors, supporting high-output tissue acquisition, site-directed delivery of model liquid or gel payloads, and active biofluid sampling under magnetic navigation. In vivo experiments in beagles demonstrated the feasibility of mechanical interventions in physiological environments. By overcoming the long-standing power and actuation constraints of capsule architecture, this work establishes a physical framework for high-output ingestible robotics and advances the development of minimally invasive robotic platforms for complex GI interventions.

item.title: Photosynthetic chimeric stem cells function as mitochondrial batteries
item.description: Therapies built on mitochondrial transfer hold promise for repairing dysfunctional, energy-deficient cells. Still, mesenchymal stem cells used as mitochondrial donors are limited by poor engraftment, risk of aberrant differentiation, and low transfer efficiency. Herein, we constructed photosynthesis-empowered cross-kingdom chimeric stem cells (PCSs; "mitochondrial battery") by introducing plant-derived thylakoid-based artificial nuclei plus FGF21-encoding messenger RNA (mRNA) into enucleated bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells. Photosynthetic activity enhances mitochondrial transfer to restore metabolism in damaged cells and elevates anabolism to increase FGF21 production. Sustained FGF21 release promotes mitochondrial biogenesis and sustains long-term cellular energy homeostasis. Mouse and porcine wound healing models demonstrate that PCSs recharge cellular energy to accelerate wound repair. This light-activated cellular photosynthetic platform supports modular mRNA programmability, shows no engraftment or aberrant differentiation, and allows repeated administration for diverse therapeutic applications.

item.title: Alleviating the stability-energy density dilemma via electron-donor-mediated orbital symmetry regulation in sodium phosphate cathodes
item.description: Manganese-based sodium super ionic conductor-type cathode materials, leveraging the multielectron redox activity of manganese, represent a promising pathway toward high-energy-density sodium-ion batteries (SIBs). However, the unavoidable generation of Mn3+(3d4) species during charge-discharge processes, characterized by asymmetric eg orbital occupancy, triggers octahedral symmetry breaking. This inherent electronic structural instability creates a fundamental contradiction between achieving high energy density and ensuring long cycle life that remains inherently difficult to reconcile. Here, we report an electron-donor-mediated (EDM) mechanism that suppresses Mn3+-induced octahedral distortion while preserving high-spin functionality. As electron-donating Fe3+ and V3+ are incorporated, Mn3+ 3d electrons undergo partial delocalization. This electronic redistribution promotes orbital interactions between neighboring transition metal sites through the transition metal-oxygen framework, driving the eg orbitals toward a more symmetric occupation and suppressing octahedral distortion. The EDM-modified cathode demonstrates a high energy density of 492.06 Wh kg-1. It delivers 178.8 mAh g-1 at 0.1 C and retains 80.2% of its capacity over 2000 cycles at 10 C, paving a novel pathway toward next-generation high-performance SIBs cathode materials.

item.title: Engineering a closed-loop electrochemical pathway for cadmium recovery and aqueous battery reutilization
item.description: Cadmium (Cd) waste is an unavoidable toxic by-product of zinc processing, but its electrochemical reutilization remains limited by the lack of routes that couple selective recovery with stable metal-anode operation. Here, we report a closed-loop electrochemical strategy that transforms model Cd-containing waste electrolytes into regenerable aqueous Cd metal anodes. A three-step potential-programmed electrodeposition process selectively recovers Cd while constructing compact Cd(002)-textured electrodes with tunable areal capacity. To preserve this recovered structure during cycling, cesium iodide is introduced to reconstruct the Cd-electrolyte interface, enabling iodide-dominated and cesium-assisted regulation of desolvation, ion flux, corrosion, and Cd growth. The resulting Cd anode achieves 99.98% average Coulombic efficiency and stable high-rate plating/stripping. Cd||I2 coin and pouch cells validate full-cell operation under high loading and reduced excess Cd. Failed Cd anodes can be reextracted, regenerated, and reused, completing a recovery-operation-regeneration loop.

item.title: A unified lattice–surface engineering strategy stabilizing oxygen redox in Li-rich cathodes for all-solid-state batteries
item.description: Li-rich Mn-based layered oxides (LRMOs) are promising high-energy cathodes for all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs), but their application is limited by irreversible O2 evolution during lattice O2-/O22- redox and interfacial degradation at high voltages. Here we report a "coat-sinter-wash" synthetic strategy that simultaneously modulates bulk oxygen redox and stabilizes the cathode surface. An ammonium tungstate precursor is first coated onto LRMO particles. The subsequent sintering generates Li vacancies and enables W incorporation into the lattice, which acts as a "chemical rivet" and enhances the reversibility of lattice oxygen redox. A final washing step reconstructs the Li-deficient surface into an in-situ spinel layer, suppressing oxygen release from the surface and mitigating structural decomposition. The resulting ASSBs achieve remarkable cycling stability with 80% capacity retention over 500 cycles (0.5 C, 25°C) and an outstanding reversible capacity of 278.2 mAh g-1 (0.1 C, 40°C). Furthermore, an all-solid-state pouch cell with Si anode demonstrates an areal capacity of 4.55 mAh cm-2 and a high energy density of 543 Wh kg-1. This work provides a scalable synthetic framework for stabilizing oxygen-redox cathodes in solid-state batteries.
